Abstract.

We study the time-asymptotic stability of solutions to the inflow problem for the one-dimensional Navier–Stokes–Fourier system on the half-line. We consider the most generic wave pattern: the superposition of a degenerate boundary layer, a rarefaction, a viscous contact wave, and a viscous shock. More precisely, if the boundary data belongs to the subsonic region, and the initial perturbation and strengths of the boundary layer, viscous contact wave, and viscous shock are sufficiently small, then the solution to the inflow problem converges to the corresponding superposition, up to a time-dependent shift for a shock. The rarefaction wave, however, is allowed to have arbitrarily large strength. To control the viscous shock, we employ the method of aa-contraction with shifts. A notable feature of our analysis is that this method can be applied even when the rarefaction wave has large amplitude. In particular, this resolves, in a generic setting, the open problem of the stability of inflow wave patterns containing a viscous shock for Navier–Stokes–Fourier system.

Key words and phrases: 
Navier–Stokes–Fourier system; Inflow problem; Riemann Problem; Viscous shock; Boundary layer; Stability

1. Introduction

We consider the inflow problem of the one-dimensional Navier–Stokes–Fourier (NSF) system on the half-line ℝ+:=(0,∞)\mathbb{R}_{+}:=(0,\infty):

(1.1) {ρt+(ρu)x=0,x≥0,t≥0,(ρ​u)t+(ρ​u2+p)x=μ​ux​x,ℰt+(u​ℰ+p​u)x=κ​θx​x+μ​(u​ux)x(ρ,u,θ)​(t,0)=(ρ−,u−,θ−)withρ−,u−,θ−>0,\begin{cases}&\rho_{t}+(\rho u)_{x}=0,\quad x\geq 0,\quad t\geq 0,\\ &(\rho u)_{t}+(\rho u^{2}+p)_{x}=\mu u_{xx},\\ &\mathcal{E}_{t}+\left(u\mathcal{E}+pu\right)_{x}=\kappa\theta_{xx}+\mu(uu_{x})_{x}\\ &(\rho,u,\theta)(t,0)=(\rho_{-},u_{-},\theta_{-})\quad\text{with}\quad\rho_{-},u_{-},\theta_{-}>0,\end{cases}

subject to the initial data

(ρ0,u0,θ0)​(x)=(ρ,u,θ)​(0,x),withinfx∈ℝ+ρ0​(x)>0,infx∈ℝ+θ0​(x)>0,(\rho_{0},u_{0},\theta_{0})(x)=(\rho,u,\theta)(0,x),\quad\text{with}\quad\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}_{+}}\rho_{0}(x)>0,\quad\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}_{+}}\theta_{0}(x)>0,

and the far-field condition

(ρ,u,θ)​(0,x)→(ρ+,u+,θ+)asx→∞.\left(\rho,u,\theta\right)(0,x)\to(\rho_{+},u_{+},\theta_{+})\quad\mbox{as}\quad{x}\to\infty.

Here, ρ=ρ⁡(t,x),u=u⁡(t,x)\rho=\rho(t,x),u=u(t,x) and θ=θ⁡(t,x)\theta=\theta(t,x) represent the fluid density, velocity and absolute temperature respectively, ℰ=ρ⁡(e+u22)\mathcal{E}=\rho(e+\frac{u^{2}}{2}) is the total energy function. For the ideal polytropic gas, the pressure function pp and the internal energy function ee are given by

p⁡(ρ,θ)=R​ρ​θ=A​ργ​exp⁡(γ−1R​s),e⁡(ρ,θ)=Rγ−1​θ+c​o​n​s​t,p(\rho,\theta)=R\rho\theta=A\rho^{\gamma}\exp\left(\frac{\gamma-1}{R}s\right),\qquad e(\rho,\theta)=\frac{R}{\gamma-1}\theta+const,

where ss is the (physical) entropy, A>0,R>0A>0,R>0, γ>1\gamma>1 being both constant related to the fluid, while μ\mu and κ\kappa denote the viscosity and the heat-conductivity.

In Lagrangian mass coordinates, the inflow problem (1.1) can be rewritten as

(1.2) {vt−ux=0,t>0,x>σ−t,ut+p​(v,θ)x=(μ​uxv)x,Et+(p⁡(v,θ)​u)x=(κ​θxv)x+(μ​u​uxv)x,(v,u,θ)​(t,σ−​t)=(v−,u−,θ−),v−,u−,θ−>0,\begin{cases}&v_{t}-u_{x}=0,\quad t>0,\quad x>\sigma_{-}t,\\ &u_{t}+p(v,\theta)_{x}=\left(\mu\frac{u_{x}}{v}\right)_{x},\\ &E_{t}+(p(v,\theta)u)_{x}=\left(\kappa\frac{\theta_{x}}{v}\right)_{x}+\left(\mu\frac{uu_{x}}{v}\right)_{x},\\ &(v,u,\theta)(t,\sigma_{-}t)=(v_{-},u_{-},\theta_{-}),\quad v_{-},u_{-},\theta_{-}>0,\end{cases}

where v⁡(t,x)=1/ρv(t,x)=1/\rho represents the specific volume, v−=1ρ−,σ−=−u−v−<0,p⁡(v,θ)=R​θvv_{-}=\frac{1}{\rho_{-}},\sigma_{-}=-\frac{u_{-}}{v_{-}}<0,p(v,\theta)=\frac{R\theta}{v}, and E=e+u22E=e+\frac{u^{2}}{2} denotes the specific total energy. Moreover, the far-field condition is reformulated by

(v,u,θ)​(0,x)→(v+,u+,θ+)asx→∞.(v,u,\theta)(0,x)\to(v_{+},u_{+},\theta_{+})\quad\mbox{as}\quad{x}\to\infty.

We are interested in the long-time dynamics of solutions U=(v,u,θ)U=(v,u,\theta) to the inflow problem (1.2). It is well known that these asymptotic patterns for the NSF system are closely related to the Riemann problem for the full Euler system (the NSF system with μ=κ=0\mu=\kappa=0). For the Cauchy problem on the whole line ℝ\mathbb{R}, one of the generic asymptotic wave patterns consists of a rarefaction wave, a viscous contact wave, a viscous shock, or their superpositions. However, for the inflow problem, an additional asymptotic pattern, namely, a boundary layer solution (stationary solution), appears due to the presence of the boundary. Indeed, the asymptotic wave patterns for the inflow problem are determined by the locations of the boundary state U−U_{-} and the far-field state U+U_{+}. To describe these wave patterns, we define the sound speed c⁡(θ)=R​γ​θc(\theta)=\sqrt{R\gamma\theta} and decompose the state space into the subsonic, transonic, and supersonic regions:

Ωs​u​b\displaystyle\Omega_{sub} :={(v,u,θ):|u|<c⁡(θ)},\displaystyle:=\{(v,u,\theta)\,:\,|u|<c(\theta)\},
Γt​r​a​n​s\displaystyle\Gamma_{trans} :={(v,u,θ):|u|=c⁡(θ)},\displaystyle:=\{(v,u,\theta)\,:\,|u|=c(\theta)\},
Ωs​u​p​e​r\displaystyle\Omega_{super} :={(v,u,θ):|u|>c⁡(θ)}.\displaystyle:=\{(v,u,\theta)\,:\,|u|>c(\theta)\}.

Since we consider the inflow problem, we restrict our attention to the regions with positive velocity and define Ωs​u​b+,Γt​r​a​n​s+\Omega_{sub}^{+},\Gamma_{trans}^{+}, and Ωs​u​p​e​r+\Omega_{super}^{+} by

Ωs​u​b+:=Ωs​u​b∩{u>0},Γt​r​a​n​s+:=Γt​r​a​n​s∩{u>0},Ωs​u​p​e​r+=Ωs​u​p​e​r∩{u>0}.\Omega_{sub}^{+}:=\Omega_{sub}\cap\{u>0\},\quad\Gamma_{trans}^{+}:=\Gamma_{trans}\cap\{u>0\},\quad\Omega_{super}^{+}=\Omega_{super}\cap\{u>0\}.

We consider the case where U−∈Ωs​u​b+U_{-}\in\Omega_{sub}^{+}. In particular, we consider the case where the asymptotic behavior of solutions to the inflow problem (1.2) is given as a superposition of a degenerate boundary layer solution, a rarefaction wave, a viscous contact wave, and a viscous shock wave, which are described below.

Before describing these waves, we first introduce the change of variables (t,ξ):=(t,x−σ−​t)(t,\xi):=(t,x-\sigma_{-}t) to fix the boundary. Then, the system (1.2) can be written in terms of (t,ξ)(t,\xi) as

(1.3) {vt−σ−vξ−uξ=0,t>0,ξ>0,ut−σ−​uξ+p​(v,θ)ξ=(μ​uξv)ξ,Et−σ−​Eξ+(p⁡(v,θ)​u)ξ=(κ​θξv)ξ+(μ​u​uξv)ξ,(v,u,θ)​(t,0)=(v−,u−,θ−),v−,u−,θ−>0,\begin{cases}&v_{t}-\sigma_{-}v_{\xi}-u_{\xi}=0,\quad t>0,\quad\xi>0,\\ &u_{t}-\sigma_{-}u_{\xi}+p(v,\theta)_{\xi}=\left(\mu\frac{u_{\xi}}{v}\right)_{\xi},\\ &E_{t}-\sigma_{-}E_{\xi}+(p(v,\theta)u)_{\xi}=\left(\kappa\frac{\theta_{\xi}}{v}\right)_{\xi}+\left(\mu\frac{uu_{\xi}}{v}\right)_{\xi},\\ &(v,u,\theta)(t,0)=(v_{-},u_{-},\theta_{-}),\quad v_{-},u_{-},\theta_{-}>0,\end{cases}

subject to the initial data and the far-field condition

(1.4) (v,u,θ)​(0,ξ)=(v0,u0,θ0)​(ξ),limξ→∞(v,u,θ)​(0,ξ)=(v+,u+,θ+).(v,u,\theta)(0,\xi)=(v_{0},u_{0},\theta_{0})(\xi),\quad\lim_{\xi\to\infty}(v,u,\theta)(0,\xi)=(v_{+},u_{+},\theta_{+}).

∙\bullet Boundary layer solution: For a given U∗∈Γt​r​a​n​s+U_{*}\in\Gamma_{trans}^{+}, [44] proved that there exists a curve Σ⊂{(u,θ):u>0,θ>0}\Sigma\subset\{(u,\theta)\,:\,u>0,\,\,\theta>0\}, such that, for any U−∈B​L​(U∗)U_{-}\in BL(U_{*}), there exists a unique (degenerate) boundary layer solution (stationary solution) UB​L=UB​L​(ξ)U^{BL}=U^{BL}(\xi) to (1.3) satisfying

(1.5) {−σ−vB​Lξ−uB​Lξ=0,ξ>0,−σ−​uξB​L+p​(vB​L,θB​L)ξ=(μ​uξB​LvB​L)ξ,−σ−​(Rγ−1​θB​L+(uB​L)22)ξ+(p⁡(vB​L,θB​L)​uB​L)ξ=(κ​θξB​LvB​L)ξ+(μ​uB​L​uξB​LvB​L)ξ,(vB​L,uB​L,θB​L)(0)=(v−,u−,θ−),(vB​L,uB​L,θB​L)(+∞)=(v∗,u∗,θ∗).\begin{cases}&-\sigma_{-}v^{BL}_{\xi}-u^{BL}_{\xi}=0,\quad\xi>0,\\ &-\sigma_{-}u^{BL}_{\xi}+p(v^{BL},\theta^{BL})_{\xi}=\left(\mu\frac{u^{BL}_{\xi}}{v^{BL}}\right)_{\xi},\\ &-\sigma_{-}\left(\frac{R}{\gamma-1}\theta^{BL}+\frac{(u^{BL})^{2}}{2}\right)_{\xi}+\big(p(v^{BL},\theta^{BL})u^{BL}\big)_{\xi}=\left(\kappa\frac{\theta^{BL}_{\xi}}{v^{BL}}\right)_{\xi}+\left(\mu\frac{u^{BL}u^{BL}_{\xi}}{v^{BL}}\right)_{\xi},\\ &(v^{BL},u^{BL},\theta^{BL})(0)=(v_{-},u_{-},\theta_{-}),\quad(v^{BL},u^{BL},\theta^{BL})(+\infty)=(v_{*},u_{*},\theta_{*}).\end{cases}

Here, the boundary layer curve B​L​(U∗)BL(U_{*}) is defined by

BL(U∗):={(v,u,θ):uv=u∗v∗=−σ−,(u,θ)∈Σ}⊂Ωs​u​b+.BL(U_{*}):=\left\{(v,u,\theta)\,:\,\frac{u}{v}=\frac{u_{*}}{v_{*}}=-\sigma_{-},\quad(u,\theta)\in\Sigma\right\}\subset\Omega_{sub}^{+}.

∙\bullet 1-rarefaction wave and approximate 1-rarefaction wave: We consider the situation in which the state U∗U_{*} and the far-field state U+U_{+} are connected by a 1-rarefaction wave, contact discontinuity, and 3-shock wave, with intermediate states UmU_{m} and U∗U^{*}. First, we consider Um∈R1​(U∗)U_{m}\in R_{1}(U_{*}), where R1​(U∗)R_{1}(U_{*}) is a 1-rarefaction curve. Namely, R1​(U∗)R_{1}(U_{*}) the integral curve of the first characteristic field:

R1(U∗):={(v,u,θ):v>v∗,s(v,θ)=s(v∗,θ∗):=s(vm,θm),\displaystyle R_{1}(U_{*}):=\bigg\{(v,u,\theta)\,:\,v>v_{*},\,\,s(v,\theta)=s(v_{*},\theta_{*}):=s(v_{m},\theta_{m}),
u=u∗−∫v∗vλ1(s∗,η)dη},\displaystyle\phantom{R_{1}(U_{*}):=\bigg\{(v,u,\theta)\,:\,\,}u=u_{*}-\int_{v_{*}}^{v}\lambda_{1}(s_{*},\eta)\,d\eta\bigg\},

where

(1.6) s⁡(v,θ)=Rγ−1​ln⁡(RA​θ​vγ−1)s(v,\theta)=\frac{R}{\gamma-1}\ln\left(\frac{R}{A}\theta v^{\gamma-1}\right)

denotes the entropy, and λ1​(s,v)=−γ​p​(v,s)v\lambda_{1}(s,v)=-\sqrt{\frac{\gamma p(v,s)}{v}} is the first eigenvalue of the Jacobian of the hyperbolic part of (1.2).

Then, for any Um∈R1​(U∗)U_{m}\in R_{1}(U_{*}), the solution to the Riemann problem of the Euler system

(1.7) {vt−ux=0,(t,x)∈ℝ+×ℝ,ut+p​(v,θ)x=0,Et+(p⁡(v,θ)​u)x=0,\begin{cases}&v_{t}-u_{x}=0,\quad(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R},\\ &u_{t}+p(v,\theta)_{x}=0,\\ &E_{t}+(p(v,\theta)u)_{x}=0,\\ \end{cases}

with the initial data

(v,u,θ)​(0,x)={(v∗,u∗,θ∗),if ​x<0,(vm,um,θm),if ​x>0,(v,u,\theta)(0,x)=\begin{cases}(v_{*},u_{*},\theta_{*}),\,\,&\text{if }x<0,\\ (v_{m},u_{m},\theta_{m}),\,\,&\text{if }x>0,\\ \end{cases}

is given by a 1-rarefaction wave Ur​(t,x)U^{r}(t,x), defined by

λ1​(vr​(t,x),θr​(t,x))={λ1​(v∗,θ∗),if ​x<λ1​(v∗,θ∗)​t,xt,if ​λ1​(v∗,θ∗)​t<x<λ1​(vm,θm)​t,λ1​(vm,θm),if ​x>λ1​(vm,θm)​t,\lambda_{1}(v^{r}(t,x),\theta^{r}(t,x))=\begin{cases}\lambda_{1}(v_{*},\theta_{*}),\,\,&\text{if }x<\lambda_{1}(v_{*},\theta_{*})t,\\ \frac{x}{t},\,\,&\text{if }\lambda_{1}(v_{*},\theta_{*})t<x<\lambda_{1}(v_{m},\theta_{m})t,\\ \lambda_{1}(v_{m},\theta_{m}),\,\,&\text{if }x>\lambda_{1}(v_{m},\theta_{m})t,\end{cases}

together with

Z1​(vr​(t,x),ur​(t,x),sr)=Z1​(v∗,u∗,sr)=Z1​(vm,um,sr),\displaystyle Z_{1}(v^{r}(t,x),u^{r}(t,x);s^{r})=Z_{1}(v_{*},u_{*};s^{r})=Z_{1}(v_{m},u_{m};s^{r}),
s⁡(vr​(t,x),θr​(t,x))=s⁡(v∗,θ∗)=s⁡(vm,θm)=:sr,\displaystyle s(v^{r}(t,x),\theta^{r}(t,x))=s(v_{*},\theta_{*})=s(v_{m},\theta_{m})=:s^{r},

where Z1​(v,u,s):=u+∫vλ1​(s,v′)​d​v′Z_{1}(v,u;s):=u+\int^{v}\lambda_{1}(s,v^{\prime})dv^{\prime}, and ss, defined in (1.6), are Riemann invariants associated with the first characteristic field.

Due to the lack of regularity of the rarefaction wave UrU^{r} at the rarefaction fronts, we introduce the following smooth approximation of UrU^{r} as in [16].

First, we define the smooth solution w⁡(t,x)=w⁡(t,x,w−,w+)w(t,x)=w(t,x;w_{-},w_{+}) of the Burgers equation

{wt+w​wx=0,w⁡(0,x)=w0​(x)={w−,x<0,w−+Cq​δr​∫0εr​xyq​e−y​dy,x≥0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}w_{t}+ww_{x}=0,\\ w(0,x)=w_{0}(x)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}w_{-},\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\,x<0,\\ w_{-}+C_{q}\delta_{r}\int^{\varepsilon_{r}x}_{0}y^{q}e^{-y}\,dy,\quad x\geq 0,\end{array}\right.\end{array}\right.

where δr=w+−w−\delta_{r}=w_{+}-w_{-}, qq is a constant satisfying q≥8q\geq 8 to be specified later, and CqC_{q} is defined by

Cq​∫0∞yq​e−y​𝑑y=1.C_{q}\int^{\infty}_{0}y^{q}e^{-y}dy=1.

Here, εr<1\varepsilon_{r}<1 is a sufficiently small constant to be chosen later.

We now construct the smooth approximate 1-rarefaction wave UA​R​(t,x)U^{AR}(t,x) corresponding to the 1-rarefaction wave Ur​(x/t)U^{r}(x/t) by

(1.13) {λ1​(vA​R,θA​R)​(t,x)=w⁡(1+t,x,λ1​((v∗,θ∗)),λ1​((vm,θm))),Z1​(vA​R​(t,x),uA​R​(t,x),sr)=Z1​(v∗,u∗,sr)=Z1​(vm,um,sr),s⁡(vA​R​(t,x),θA​R​(t,x))=s⁡(v∗,θ∗)=s⁡(vm,θm)=sr.\begin{cases}&\lambda_{1}(v^{AR},\theta^{AR})(t,x)=w(1+t,x;\lambda_{1}((v_{*},\theta_{*})),\lambda_{1}((v_{m},\theta_{m}))),\\ &Z_{1}(v^{AR}(t,x),u^{AR}(t,x);s^{r})=Z_{1}(v_{*},u_{*};s^{r})=Z_{1}(v_{m},u_{m};s^{r}),\\ &s(v^{AR}(t,x),\theta^{AR}(t,x))=s(v_{*},\theta_{*})=s(v_{m},\theta_{m})=s^{r}.\end{cases}

Then, one can verify that the approximate 1-rarefaction wave UA​RU^{AR} satisfies the Euler system (1.7). Moreover, UA​RU^{AR} indeed approximates the self-similar rarefaction wave UrU^{r} in the sense that (see Lemma 2.3):

supx∈ℝ|(vA​R,uA​R,θA​R)​(t,x)−(vr,ur,θr)​(x1+t)|→0ast→∞.\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\left|(v^{AR},u^{AR},\theta^{AR})(t,x)-(v^{r},u^{r},\theta^{r})\left(\frac{x}{1+t}\right)\right|\to 0\quad\text{as}\quad t\to\infty.

We then define a approximate 1-rarefaction wave URU^{R} on the half-line ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+} as the restriction of UA​RU^{AR}:

(1.14) (vR,uR,θR)​(t,ξ):=(vA​R,uA​R,θA​R)​(t,ξ+σ−​t).(v^{R},u^{R},\theta^{R})(t,\xi):=(v^{AR},u^{AR},\theta^{AR})(t,\xi+\sigma_{-}t).

∙\bullet Viscous contact wave: Next, we consider U∗∈C​D​(Um)U^{*}\in CD(U_{m}), where C​D​(Um)CD(U_{m}) denotes the 2-contact discontinuity curve defined by

(1.15) CD(Um):={(v,u,θ):u=um,p(v,θ)=p(vm,θm)}.CD(U_{m}):=\big\{(v,u,\theta)\,:\,u=u_{m},\,\,p(v,\theta)=p(v_{m},\theta_{m})\big\}.

Since the second characteristic field of the Euler system (1.7) is linearly degenerate, the corresponding Riemann solution for the Euler system (1.7) with the initial data

(v,u,θ)​(0,x)={(vm,um,θm),if ​x<0,(v∗,u∗,θ∗),if ​x>0,(v,u,\theta)(0,x)=\begin{cases}(v_{m},u_{m},\theta_{m}),\quad&\text{if }x<0,\\ (v^{*},u^{*},\theta^{*}),\quad&\text{if }x>0,\end{cases}

is given by a contact discontinuity UcU^{c} defined by

(vc,uc,θc)​(t,x)={(vm,um,θm),if ​x<0,(v∗,u∗,θ∗),if ​x>0.(v^{c},u^{c},\theta^{c})(t,x)=\begin{cases}(v_{m},u_{m},\theta_{m}),\quad&\text{if }x<0,\\ (v^{*},u^{*},\theta^{*}),\quad&\text{if }x>0.\end{cases}

In the viscous setting, for any U∗∈C​D​(Um)U^{*}\in CD(U_{m}), we define a viscous contact wave UV​C​(t,x)U^{VC}(t,x) on ℝ\mathbb{R} associated with the contact discontinuity UcU^{c} by

Remark 1.2.
  1. (1)

    Theorem 1.1 requires the strengths of BL solution, viscous contact wave, and viscous shock wave to be small and bounded by the constant δ0\delta_{0}, which does not depend on ε0\varepsilon_{0} the smallness of the initial perturbation. However, the rarefaction strength need not be small. Unlike the barotropic Navier–Stokes system as in [11, 35], little is known about explicit formula of the boundary layer curve. So, it is natural to define the boundary layer curve starting from the given right state U∗U_{*} via the center-stable manifold.

  2. (2)

    The assumption 1<γ≤21<\gamma\leq 2 is physically natural. For an ideal gas, the adiabatic exponent is determined by the number of effective molecular degrees of freedom; in particular, ordinary gases have at least three translational degrees of freedom, leading to γ≤5/3<2\gamma\leq 5/3<2. More generally, additional rotational or vibrational modes only decrease γ\gamma, so the range 1<γ≤21<\gamma\leq 2 covers the physically relevant regimes. Technically, the restriction 1<γ≤21<\gamma\leq 2 is only required in the proof for the monotonicity (5.33) of vR​θRv^{R}\theta^{R} that is used to get a sharp estimate for the diffusion term despite the large strength of a rarefaction wave.

  3. (3)

    We first shift the viscous shock profile by a sufficiently large constant β>0\beta>0, which is sufficiently larger than the reciprocal of shock strength. That is, we consider the initial location of shock front sufficiently far from the boundary by O⁡(β)O(\beta). This allows us to control the discrepancy between the prescribed boundary data and the boundary values of the viscous shock profile. This, in turn, guarantees the stability of the viscous shock under sufficiently small perturbations.

  4. (4)

    The L2L^{2}-norm of the initial perturbation is measured relative to the shift β\beta, since the viscous shock is located far from the origin by β\beta-scale. Moreover, since the strength of a rarefaction wave is large, while the initial perturbation is small, the approximate rarefaction URU^{R} is included in all the norms appearing in the initial perturbation.

  5. (5)

    Since the speed of shift X⁡(t)X(t) vanishes in the limit as t→∞t\to\infty, the shifted shock wave would time-asymptotically belong to one-parameter family of shock waves. However, we do not ensure the final destination of shift, since we do not guarantee the existence of limt→+∞X⁡(t)\displaystyle\lim_{t\rightarrow+\infty}X(t).

1.2. Previous Results

There have been extensive studies on the well-posedness of hyperbolic systems of conservation laws and viscous conservation laws. For scalar conservation laws, Bardos, le Roux, and Nédélec [4] extended the Kružkov theory [34] to initial-boundary value problems by introducing an appropriate entropy boundary condition. We also refer to [37, 43] for further developments on boundary conditions and traces. For systems of conservation laws, Amadori [1] proved the existence of small BV entropy solutions, with the boundary condition determined by the whole-space Riemann problem, allowing for characteristic boundaries. Later, Amadori and Colombo [2] constructed the Standard Riemann Semigroup for 2×22\times 2 systems, and Donadello and Marson [7] subsequently extended this construction to N×NN\times N systems with non-characteristic boundaries. More recently, Ancona, Marson, and Spinolo [3] showed the existence of small BV solutions satisfying a boundary condition consistent with the vanishing-viscosity approximation, building on the boundary-layer analyses in [5, 6].

We next turn to viscous conservation laws. In initial-boundary value problems, boundary effects may give rise to nontrivial stationary solutions as possible asymptotic states. We refer to [13, 21, 31, 32, 33, 41, 42] for studies of stationary solutions for the compressible Navier–Stokes system and related systems in one and several space dimensions. In the one-dimensional inflow setting, the associated boundary Riemann problem for the corresponding Euler system, as characterized in [3, 5], determines the asymptotic wave pattern of the Navier–Stokes system (see also [35]). For the isentropic Navier–Stokes (NS) system, Matsumura and Nishihara [36] established the stability of BL solutions, rarefaction waves, and their superpositions. Later, Fan, Liu, Wang, and Zhao [9] extended these stability results for boundary layer solutions (stationary solutions) and rarefaction waves to allow initial perturbations with large oscillations.

For the NSF system, Huang, Li, and Shi [15] proved the stability of boundary layers, rarefaction waves, and their superpositions. Qin and Wang [38] established the stability of superpositons consisting of a nondegnerate BL solution, rarefaction waves, and a viscous contact wave. Subsequently, Qin and Wang [39] extended this result to the case of a degenerate BL solution.

Regarding viscous shock waves in the NS system, Huang, Matsumura, and Shi [17] proved the stability of a superposition of a boundary layer solution and a viscous shock by employing the antiderivative method and by introducing the modified variable. However, the stability of wave patterns including a viscous shock in the inflow problem for the NSF system has remained open. In contrast to the classical antiderivative method used in earlier works, the method of aa-contraction with shifts provides an alternative framework for studying initial-boundary value problems for the compressible Navier–Stokes system (see, for example, [11, 19, 23]). In this paper, we employ the method of aa-contraction with shifts to resolve the open problem on the long-time behavior toward an asymptotic pattern containing a shock wave. More importantly, our asymptotic pattern consists of a degenerate boundary layer solution, a rarefaction wave, a viscous contact wave, and a viscous shock. We emphasize that this is the most generic asymptotic pattern containing a shock.

1.3. Idea of Proof

The main part of the proof is devoted to deriving the L2L^{2}-estimates for perturbations. In the whole-space setting, the L2L^{2}-distance provides, as in [29], a unified framework for establishing the stability of small perturbations around a composite wave consisting of a rarefaction wave, a viscous contact wave, and a viscous shock wave. So, we employ the same L2L^{2}-framework for the initial-boundary value problem considered in the present paper. The key ingredient of the L2L^{2}-framework is the method of aa-contraction with shifts (in short, the aa-contraction method), which provides a robust method for controlling perturbations around viscous shock waves. This method has been successfully applied to establish contraction properties for viscous shocks on the half-line in [11, 19, 23] (see also [8, 10, 12, 20, 22, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29] for the whole-space setting).

To derive the zeroth-order estimates, we employ a weighted relative entropy functional with a temporal shift to control the perturbation around the composite wave under the a priori assumption of smallness. The weight is chosen according to the viscous shock profile as defined in (3.2), while the time evolution of the weighted relative entropy provides the fundamental dissipative structure established in Lemma 5.2. In addition, the temporal shift is defined as the average of a localized perturbation, which enables us to control the bad terms localized near the shock through the aa-contraction method.

More precisely, the main difficulties in establishing the zeroth-order energy estimates are as follows.

As the core of the aa-contraction method, we first maximize the relative entropy flux and then apply the change of variables ξ↦y\xi\mapsto y defined by (5.27) to the leading-order terms associated with the modulation term (induced by the temporal shift), the diffusion terms, and the hyperbolic terms localized by the derivatives of the shock profile (or equivalently, the weight function). Under this transformation, these leading-order contributions are reduced to quantities that can be controlled by the Poincaré-type inequality stated in Lemma 2.6.
Unlike the previous works based on the aa-contraction method, however, the main difficulty in the present problem arises from the fact that the rarefaction wave is not assumed to have small strength. In particular, this creates a serious obstacle when reducing the diffusion term

Dθ1:=κ​∫av​θ​|(θ−θ¯)ξ|2​𝑑ξD_{\theta_{1}}:=\kappa\int\frac{a}{v\theta}|(\theta-\bar{\theta})_{\xi}|^{2}\,d\xi

to the favorable form

∫y01(y−y0)​(1−y)​|(θ−θ¯)y|2​𝑑y\int_{y_{0}}^{1}(y-y_{0})(1-y)|(\theta-\bar{\theta})_{y}|^{2}\,dy

which appears in Lemma 2.6, through the Jacobian estimates for d​y/d​ξdy/d\xi established in Lemma 5.8. Indeed, because the rarefaction wave may have large amplitude, the coefficient 1/(v​θ)1/(v\theta) is no longer uniformly close to 1/(vS​θS)1/(v^{S}\theta^{S}). On the other hand, the Jacobian estimates depend only on the viscous shock profile and therefore do not directly capture the effect of the rarefaction wave.

To overcome this difficulty, we observe a delicate monotonicity property of the quantity vS​θSv^{S}\theta^{S}, established in (5.33), which holds for 1<γ≤21<\gamma\leq 2. This property follows from the explicit representation of the entropy in (1.6), together with the fact that the rarefaction wave preserves the entropy. As a consequence, the mismatch between the diffusion coefficient and the Jacobian can still be controlled, allowing us to recover the favorable diffusion structure required for the Poincaré-type inequality.

Second, another major difficulty arises in estimating the interactions among the wave components, since the boundary layer is degenerate and the rarefaction wave is allowed to have large strength. In the present problem, we consider a degenerate boundary layer whose right state lies on the transonic curve. Unlike the non-degenerate case, such a boundary layer exhibits only algebraic decay toward the far field, as shown in Lemma 2.1. Consequently, its interactions with the other wave components decay much more slowly and therefore require a more delicate analysis.

A further difficulty stems from the large-amplitude rarefaction wave. To control its interactions with the other wave components, we introduce a smooth approximate rarefaction profile parameterized by a small parameter εr\varepsilon_{r}, whose transition layer has thickness of order εr−1\varepsilon_{r}^{-1}. This construction ensures that the derivatives of the approximate rarefaction are sufficiently small. The parameter εr\varepsilon_{r} is then chosen appropriately so that all interaction terms involving the rarefaction wave remain sufficiently small. In this way, the approximation error of the smooth rarefaction profile and the nonlinear interaction terms can be balanced simultaneously within the stability analysis.

Third, a fundamental difficulty in the analysis of the initial-boundary value problem arises from the boundary terms generated by integration by parts. For the rarefaction wave constructed in (2.4), its boundary value coincides with its left state U∗U_{*}, so this component produces no boundary mismatch. Consequently, the boundary discrepancies arise only from the viscous contact wave and the viscous shock. For the viscous contact wave, the inflow structure implies that its boundary discrepancy decays exponentially in time, as shown in (5.46). In particular, it is bounded by the contact wave strength δC\delta_{C}. For the viscous shock, the a priori estimate for the temporal shift implies that |X˙​(t)||\dot{X}(t)| remains sufficiently small, so that the propagation speed of the shifted shock stays close to the Rankine–Hugoniot speed. Combined with the exponential decay of the viscous shock profile, this yields a small boundary discrepancy. More precisely, the discrepancy can be bounded by e−c​δS​βe^{-c\delta_{S}\beta}, provided that the initial shock location β\beta is chosen sufficiently large compared to δS−1\delta_{S}^{-1}.

Finally, by applying an interpolation inequality, we show that all boundary terms can be controlled by these small boundary discrepancies together with the diffusion terms. Consequently, the boundary contributions can be absorbed into the energy estimates.

1.4. Organization of the Paper

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we provide the useful quantitative properties of the boundary layer solution, rarefaction wave, viscous contact wave, and viscous shock. In Section 3, we state the local existence result and formulate the a priori estimates. Section 4 is devoted to estimates of the interactions between the boundary layer and the elementary waves. In Section 5 and Section 6, we establish the L2L^{2}- and H1H^{1}- energy estimates for the perturbation between the solutions to the inflow problem (1.3) and the superposed wave profile U¯\overline{U}, thereby completing the proof of Proposition 3.2.

2. Preliminaries

In this section, we provide several fundamental properties of the basic wave patterns, namely BL solutions, (approximate) rarefaction waves, viscous contact waves, and viscous shock waves. We also present a one-dimensional Poincaré-type inequality on any compact interval, which is a key ingredient in deriving the L2L^{2} energy estimates localized by a viscous shock wave.

3.4. Proof of Theorem 1.1

Based on Proposition 3.1 and Proposition 3.2, we use a continuity argument to prove the global existence result (1.20) for the inflow problem. The detailed proof of (1.20) is deferred to the Appendix C.

In addition, the time-asymptotic stability (1.22) can be proved by showing that

‖(v−v¯,u−u¯,θ−θ¯)ξ​(t,⋅)‖L2​(ℝ+)2∈W1,1​(ℝ+).\|(v-\bar{v},u-\bar{u},\theta-\bar{\theta})_{\xi}(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{+})}^{2}\in W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}_{+}).

Since the proof of (1.22) is standard and similar to that in [11], we omit the details.

Finally, (1.23) directly follows from (3.1) and (1.22).

3.5. Notations

The following sections are devoted to proving Proposition 3.2. In what follows, we omit the spatial domain ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+} whenever there is no confusion. For example, we write LpL^{p} and H1H^{1} for Lp​(ℝ+)L^{p}(\mathbb{R}_{+}) and H1​(ℝ+)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+}), respectively. Moreover, we introduce the following notations:

and

and for any t∈[0,T0]t\in[0,T_{0}] and ξ∈ℝ+\xi\in\mathbb{R}_{+},

min⁡{v−,v+}4<v⁡(t,x)<4​max​{v−,v+},min⁡{θ−,θ+}4<θ⁡(t,x)<4​max​{θ−,θ+}.\frac{\min\{v_{-},v_{+}\}}{4}<v(t,x)<4\max\{v_{-},v_{+}\},\,\,\frac{\min\{\theta_{-},\theta_{+}\}}{4}<\theta(t,x)<4\max\{\theta_{-},\theta_{+}\}.

We now show that the solution can be globally extended by using the standard continuation argument. To this end, we define the maximal existence time

TM:=sup{T>0|supt∈[0,T]‖(v−v¯,u−u¯,θ−θ¯)​(t,⋅)‖H1​(ℝ+)≤ε}.T_{M}:=\sup\left\{T>0~\Bigg|~\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\|(v-\bar{v},u-\bar{u},\theta-\bar{\theta})(t,\cdot)\|_{H^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})}\leq\varepsilon\right\}.

Suppose, for the contradiction, that TMT_{M} is finite. Then, by the definition of TMT_{M}, we have

supt∈[0,TM]‖(v−v¯,u−u¯,θ−θ¯)​(t,⋅)‖H1​(ℝ+)=ε.\sup_{t\in[0,T_{M}]}\|(v-\bar{v},u-\bar{u},\theta-\bar{\theta})(t,\cdot)\|_{H^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})}=\varepsilon.

On the other hand, using (C.2) and (C.4), we find that

‖(v0−v¯​(0,⋅),u0−u¯​(0,⋅),θ0−θ¯​(0,⋅))‖H1​(ℝ+)<ε∗+C^1​δ0=ε2​(C0+1)−δ01/40−e−c​δS​β.\displaystyle\|(v_{0}-\bar{v}(0,\cdot),u_{0}-\bar{u}(0,\cdot),\theta_{0}-\bar{\theta}(0,\cdot))\|_{H^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})}<\varepsilon_{*}+\hat{C}_{1}\sqrt{\delta_{0}}=\frac{\varepsilon}{2(C_{0}+1)}-\delta_{0}^{1/40}-e^{-c\delta_{S}\beta}.

Then, Proposition 3.2 implies that

supt∈[0,TM](‖v−v¯‖H1​(ℝ+)+‖u−u¯‖H1​(ℝ+))≤ε2,\sup_{t\in[0,T_{M}]}\left(\|v-\bar{v}\|_{H^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})}+\|u-\bar{u}\|_{H^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})}\right)\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2},

which is a contradiction. Therefore, we deduce TM=+∞T_{M}=+\infty, and the a priori estimate (3.5) holds for the whole time interval [0,∞)[0,\infty).
